```{r}
library("tidyverse")
library("broom")
```

## Loading output data from 03_augment

```{r}
# Load datasets into environment
data_path <- "../data/"

pam50_augmented <- read_tsv(str_c(data_path, 
                                  "03_dat_augment_pam50_filtered.tsv"), 
                                 show_col_types = FALSE)
all_genes_augmented  <- read_tsv(str_c(data_path, 
                                       "03_dat_augment_all_genes.tsv"), 
                             show_col_types = FALSE)
```

# Analysis

## Principal Component Analysis

We begin ensuring that our data is in wide format

```{r}
pca_wide <- all_genes_augmented |> 
  filter(`PAM50 mRNA` != "control") |> 
  rename(subtype= `PAM50 mRNA`) |> 
  select(patient_id, subtype, matches("^[NXY]P_"))
```

Using the GeeksForGeeks PCA tutorial listed in the references, we carry out PCA with centering, scaling, and retx.

```{r}
pca_res <- pca_wide |> 
  select(-patient_id, -subtype) |> 
  prcomp(scale.=TRUE, center=TRUE, retx=TRUE)
```

### Captured variance per principal component

The following two chunks of code will help us observe how much variance is captured by each of the PCs. Then, we will also observe the PC loadings for a couple of proteins.

```{r}
pca_res |> 
  tidy(matrix = "eigenvalues") |>
  slice_head(n=10)
```

```{r}
pca_res |> 
  tidy(matrix = "loadings") |> 
  filter(PC <= 4) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = PC, 
              names_prefix = "PC", 
              values_from = value) |> 
  slice_head(n=5)
```

Before continuing, we will add a chunk of code that will be useful to extract the labels to avoid using base R. This will be needed in a couple of our following steps.

```{r}
pc_var <- pca_res |> 
  tidy(matrix="eigenvalues") |> 
  mutate(label = str_c("PC", PC, "(", round(percent*100, 1), "%)"))

#Now we extract the labels to avoid using base R
extract_label <- function (pca_n){
  pc_var |> 
    filter(PC == pca_n) |> 
    pull(label)
}

pc1_label <- extract_label(1)
pc2_label <- extract_label(2)

```

### PCA scatterplot in two dimensions

Now, we are making a scatterplot colored by subtype to help us answer the if tumors belonging to the same subtype share proteins. If the subtypes properly separate, then we could argue that proteins seem to distinguish the subtypes; whereas if they're all scattered, then the proteins aren't enough to do so. Also, the groups that are placed closer to one another will have similar profiles.

```{r}
pca_scores <- pca_res |> 
  augment(data = pca_wide) |> 
  rename_with(\(x) str_remove(x, "\\.fitted"),
              starts_with(".fitted")) |> 
  select(patient_id, 
         subtype, 
         starts_with("PC"))


pca_scores |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, color = subtype)) +
  geom_point(size=3, alpha=0.8) +
  labs(title = "PCA of breast tumors proteomes", 
       x = pc1_label, 
       y = pc2_label, 
       color ="PAM50 subtype") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Proteins with gene names that pull basal-like tumors to the top of the plot.

After having observed the scatterplot, we notice that in two dimensions, the patients with basal-like breast cancer separate on the top of the plot. Meanwhile, the rest of the patients sit in a continuum. Now we will see which proteins (with their gene names) have a greater magnitude in principal component 2. We are only focusing on PC2, because it's precisely in that direction where basal-like tumors spread, and we want to figure what is separating that subtype from the other three.

```{r}
gene_names <- read_csv("../data/_raw/77_cancer_proteomes_CPTAC_itraq.csv",
                       show_col_types=FALSE) |> 
  select(RefSeq_accession_number, gene_symbol, gene_name) |> 
  distinct()

top_pc2 <- pca_res |> 
  tidy(matrix = "loadings") |> 
  filter(PC == 2) |> 
  slice_max(abs(value), n=10) |> 
  left_join(gene_names, by=c("column"="RefSeq_accession_number")) |> 
  select(column, gene_symbol, gene_name, value)

top_pc2
```

A very interesting remark is that, proteins with large-magnitude PC2 loadings included FOXA1. This is a characteristic transcription factor found in luminal breast cancer, with less presence in basal-like tumors (Kumar, et al., 2021). This is consistent with the separation of basal-like tumors along this axis.

## K-means

Now, we will carry out k-means clustering (with and without PAM50) to understand why it makes sense to use PAM50 proteins to distinguish subtypes rather than using the rest of the proteome as well. Right now, we have the PCA scatterplot, but a K-means will help us explore further. Once again, this is based on a GeeksForGeeks tutorial.

### Slight preprocessing to split the protein columns (with and without PAM50).

```{r}
pam50_ids <- read_csv("../data/_raw/PAM50_proteins.csv",
                      show_col_types=FALSE) |> 
  pull(RefSeqProteinID)

pam50_only <- pca_wide |> 
  select(any_of(pam50_ids))

no_pam50 <- pca_wide |> 
  select(-patient_id, -subtype, -any_of(pam50_ids))
```

Finally, we can carry out the k-means clustering. We are using k = 4 to match the four PAM50 subtypes

```{r}
set.seed(42) #to ensure reproducibility 

kmeans_clust <- function(proteins){
  kmeans(proteins, centers = 4, nstart=20)
}

km_pam50 <- kmeans_clust(pam50_only)
km_nopam50 <- kmeans_clust(no_pam50)
```

We can compare the clusters we obtained with the known subtypes. The next chunks will help us visualize the cluster plots. It is important to mention that this plot will combine both the PC scores together with the results obtained by k-means.

```{r}
pca_kmeans <- pca_scores |> 
  bind_cols(
    augment(km_pam50, pam50_only) |> 
      select(cluster_pam50 = .cluster),
    augment(km_nopam50, no_pam50) |> 
      select(cluster_nopam50 = .cluster)
    )
```

### Subtype counts per cluster for the two approaches

```{r}
pca_kmeans |> 
  count(subtype, cluster_pam50) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = cluster_pam50,
              values_from = n,
              values_fill = 0)

pca_kmeans |> 
  count(subtype, cluster_nopam50) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = cluster_nopam50,
              values_from = n,
              values_fill=0)

```

### Cluster plots with and without PAM50

```{r}
#Clusters from the PAM50 proteins
pca_kmeans |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, color = cluster_pam50, shape=subtype)) +
  geom_point(size=3, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group=cluster_pam50)) +
  labs(title = "K-means clusters (PAM50 proteins)",
       x = pc1_label,
       y= pc2_label,
       color = "K-means (PAM50 proteins)",
       shape = "PAM50 subtype") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#Clusters for the rest of the proteome minus the PAM50 proteins
pca_kmeans |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, color = cluster_nopam50, shape=subtype)) +
  geom_point(size=3, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = cluster_nopam50)) +
  labs(title = "K-means (without PAM50)",
       x = pc1_label,
       y = pc2_label, 
       color = "K-means (without PAM50)",
       shape = "PAM50 subtype") +
  theme_minimal()
```

So far, the PAM50 proteins appear to separate basal-like tumors more cleanly than when carrying out k-means without these proteins. The counts reveal that 17 of 18 basal like samples fall in a single cluster versus 13 of 18 without PAM50; however, HER2-enriched and luminal samples are consistently mixed across clusters in both cases. It is important to distinguish that the PAM50 set contains a few protein, whereas the rest of the proteome has thousands, so the difference could be due to set size and not to the PAM50 proteins themselves.

## Purity scores

As a final part of the analysis, we will explore the purity scores for the two approaches we've been working with. The way this works is that, for each cluster, we take the tumor subtype more common and calculate the proportion of patients in said cluster that belongs to its main subtype. Since the PAM50 set has far fewer proteins than the rest of the proteome, we will compare its purity against 100 random sets of proteins of the same size.

```{r}
n_pam50 <- ncol(pam50_only)
subtypes <- pull(pca_wide, subtype)

n_pam50
```

### Definition of the function to calculate purity

```{r}
cluster_purity <- function(subtypes, clusters){
  counts <- tibble(subtypes, clusters) |> 
    count(clusters, subtypes)
  #The following part is to know the amount of patients in total
  n_total <- counts |> 
    summarise(s = sum(n)) |> 
    pull(s)
  
  counts |> 
    slice_max(n, by=clusters, with_ties=FALSE) |> 
    summarise(purity = sum(n) / n_total) |> #This is the calculation itself!
    pull(purity)
}
```

### Calculating purity for 100 random samples of proteins (no PAM50)

```{r}
random_purity <- function(n_proteins){
  chosen <- tibble(protein = names(no_pam50)) |> 
    slice_sample(n=n_proteins) |> 
    pull(protein)
  
  random_set <- no_pam50 |> 
    select(all_of(chosen))
  
  clusters <- kmeans_clust(random_set) |> 
    augment(random_set) |> 
    pull(.cluster)
  
  cluster_purity(subtypes, clusters)
}
```

```{r}
set.seed(42)
random_scores <- tibble(rep = 1:100) |>  #the process is repeated 100 times
  mutate(purity = map_dbl(rep, \(i) random_purity(n_pam50)))
```

### Purity for clusters with PAM50

```{r}
purity_pam50 <- cluster_purity(subtypes, pull(pca_kmeans, cluster_pam50)) 
purity_pam50
```

### Empirical p-value

We'll calculate it as the mean of the amount of times our random samples (without PAM50) had a purity higher or equal to that of the clusters in which PAM50 proteins were used.

```{r}
random_scores |> 
  summarise(p_empirical = mean(purity >= purity_pam50 ))
```

### Histogram plot comparing purity distributions vs. PAM50 purity score

Fianlly, we can create a histogram to see how the purity score of the 100 random set of proteins is distributed in comparison to the PAM50 set purity score!

```{r}
random_scores |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=purity))+
  geom_histogram(bins=20) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = purity_pam50, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title="Purity of random protein sets vs. PAM50",
       x = "Purity score", 
       y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

As observed, none of the 100 random sets reached the purity of the PAM50 proteins. This is backed up by an empirical p-value \< 0.01, which suggests that the advantage of the PAM50 proteins is not explaines by the set size alone.

## Results

As we observed, basal-like tumors separate from the rest of the subtypes in the PCA. This happens mostly in the second principal component, while HER2-enriched and luminal types form a continuum that overlaps. FOXA1 is among the proteins with the largest magnitude in PC2 with a negative loading opposite to the direction where basal-like observations are spread. This is a luminal marker, so it is consistent with the separation. Other proteins such as LYN, MYO1F and MSN point towards basal-like tumors.

Using k-means (k=4), basal-like is the subtype that was recovered best with 17/18 samples in the same cluster with PAM50 and 13/18 without PAM50. HER2-enriched and the luminal subtypes are mixed in both cases, so the proteome is not able to properly "separate" the 4 subtypes.

Purity is greater with PAM50 than without those proteins (\~0.61). This advantage is not explained only by the set size of the PAM50 subset, as none of the 100 random sets of proteins with equal size reached the purity that PAM50 yielded (p\<0.01).

### Limitations

Of course, this is not a discovery per se, since PAM50 proteins were selected to distinguish these subtypes, but instead works as a confirmation of this design. Separation is moderate and is mainly observed for basal-like tumors. Also, better results could come from having a greater sample of patients.
